# .gitlab-ci.yml
build:
  script:
    - nix build
    - nix path-info -Shr ./result
    - nix-store -q --tree ./result | head -40
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - result
    expire_in: 1 day
The result symlink as an artifact is not a closure. It is a pointer that will not work on a machine without /nix. Use nix copy --to file://$PWD/nar and artifact nar/ if humans must download.

title: GitLab CI Integration
text:
The trap
The trap is image: ubuntu:24.04 plus curl | sh the Nix installer on every job. You pay minutes and get a different Nix version than last week. Use a Nix image or a Nix-equipped runner.
The other trap is caching only result in GitLab artifacts and calling it a binary cache. Artifacts are not signed NARs.

title: GitLab CI Integration
text:
The boring rule

Pin nixos/nix:<version> or use a self-hosted runner that already has Nix.
NIX_CONFIG enables flakes inside the job.
Same team cache as GitHub Actions and laptops.
Write tokens only on the default branch.
nix path-info -Shr in the log so a fat closure is visible in review.

title: GitLab CI Integration
text:
Try this

Run Case 1 against a flake that builds hello. Confirm the job log contains Hello or a store path for hello.
Pin the image digest (nixos/nix:2.35.2@sha256:…) and record why that is stricter than a moving tag.
Add nix path-info -Shr ./result and paste the closure size into the merge request template once.
On a self-hosted runner, run nix-collect-garbage --delete-older-than 7d after a week and note df -h /nix.

title: Build Caching Strategies
text:
Build Caching Strategies
CI that recompiles llvm because someone edited README.md is not a pipeline, it is a heater. The boring default is: substituters first, a persistent team cache second, GitHub’s cache API only as a bump, and src filters so docs do not bust compiles.

title: Build Caching Strategies
text:
Mental model
Nix does not cache “step 3 of a Dockerfile.” It caches store paths. If the .drv hash is unchanged, the path is substituted. If src includes the whole git tree, every commit is a new .drv.
Layers, cheapest first:








Layer
Lifetime
Who uses it




Local /nix/store
Until GC
This runner / laptop


Team cache (Cachix / Attic)
Months
Every laptop + every CI job


magic-nix-cache (GHA)
Days, per repo
GitHub-hosted runners only



Docker layer cache busts everything after a changed line. Nix rebuilds only the node whose inputs moved, plus dependents. A docs derivation and a Go derivation are siblings, not a stack.
README.md change
   ├── hello-docs.drv   rebuilt
   └── desk-api.drv     same hash → substitute

title: Build Caching Strategies
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Team cache is the real cache
The binary-cache chapter already added substituters. CI must push what it built:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: cachix/install-nix-action@v27
      - uses: cachix/cachix-action@v15
        with:
          name: desk-cache
          authToken: ${{ secrets.CACHIX_AUTH_TOKEN }}
      - run: nix build --print-build-logs
A laptop with the same flake.lock then substitutes. magic-nix-cache alone does not help the laptop.


Case 2: magic-nix-cache as a spare tyre
# .github/workflows/ci-magic.yml
name: CI
on: [push]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: DeterminateSystems/nix-installer-action@v16
      - uses: DeterminateSystems/magic-nix-cache-action@v8
      - run: nix build
Fine for a personal repo. Evicts. Does not sign NARs for other machines. Graduate to Cachix when a second human waits on CI.


Case 3: lib.cleanSource / gitignore
Save as package.nix:
# package.nix
{ pkgs ? import <nixpkgs> {} }:

pkgs.stdenv.mkDerivation {
  pname = "desk-banner";
  version = "1.0.0";
  src = pkgs.lib.cleanSource ./.;
  buildPhase = "echo ok > $out";
  installPhase = "true";
}
cleanSource drops .git, result, and editor junk. Stricter:
src = pkgs.lib.cleanSourceWith {
  src = ./.;
  filter = path: type:
    baseNameOf path != "README.md"
    && baseNameOf path != "docs";
};
Or pkgs.nix-gitignore.gitignoreSource [ ] ./. with a .gitignore you actually maintain.
nix-build package.nix
echo "# note" >> README.md
nix-build package.nix
If the second build is “checking paths” / a cache hit, the filter worked. If it rebuilds, README.md is still in src.


Case 4: Vendor once, compile often
Save as go.nix:
# go.nix
{ pkgs ? import <nixpkgs> {} }:

pkgs.buildGoModule {
  pname = "desk-api";
  version = "1.0.0";
  src = pkgs.lib.cleanSource ./.;
  vendorHash = "sha256-AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=";
}
vendorHash is a FOD. Changing main.go does not re-fetch modules. Changing go.mod does. Probe the hash once; do not set vendorHash = null in CI “to make it work.”


Case 5: See what would rebuild
nix build --dry-run
nix path-info -Shr ./result | tail -1
--dry-run lists derivations that are not in the store or substituters. If that list includes gcc after a comment-only change, src is too wide or an input leaked (currentTime, impure env).

title: Build Caching Strategies
text:
The trap
The trap is src = ./. on a monorepo root for a leaf package. A frontend CSS change rebuilds the Go API. Filter to ./cmd/desk-api or fileset (lib.fileset.gitTracked).
The other trap is treating GHA cache as the team cache. A new contributor’s first nix build still compiles the world.

title: Build Caching Strategies
text:
The boring rule

Push to a signed team cache from trusted CI. Laptops pull.
Filter src. Docs and .git are not compile inputs.
Language vendor hashes (Go, Cargo, npm) are FODs. Pin them.
--dry-run after a trivial edit. If gcc is in the list, stop and fix inputs.
magic-nix-cache is optional. Substituters are not.

title: Build Caching Strategies
text:
Try this

nix path-info -Shr ./result before and after a README-only commit. The store path of the binary should be identical if src is filtered.
--dry-run twice in a row with no edits. Second list should be empty (or only substitutes).
Break vendorHash by one character, watch the FOD mismatch, restore it.
Time nix build on a clean store with the team cache configured versus nix build --option substituters ''. The delta is the cache earning its keep.

title: Testing in CI Pipelines
text:
Testing in CI Pipelines
Tests that need the office Wi-Fi are not tests. The boring default is: hermetic checkPhase / go test inside the derivation, nix flake check on every PR against nixpkgs 26.05, and NixOS VM tests when a unit must listen.

title: Testing in CI Pipelines
text:
Mental model
The sandbox has no network. go test that downloads modules fails. vendorHash (FOD) already fetched modules. npm test that hits staging fails. Mock it.



Kind
Where




Unit
doCheck / checkPhase on the package


Lint
checks.<system>.lint


Integration
testers.runNixOSTest (needs KVM)


Gate
nix flake check -L in CI



GitHub Actions: install Nix 2.35 (or the 26.05-pinned Nix), then nix flake check. No setup-go.

title: Testing in CI Pipelines
Testing in CI Pipelines
text:
The trap
The trap is go test that hits https://staging.desk.internal. Sandbox: connection refused. “Works on my laptop” because your laptop is not a sandbox. doCheck must be hermetic. Integration against staging is a deploy job with secrets, not flake check.

title: Testing in CI Pipelines
text:
The boring rule

nix flake check -L is the PR gate. 26.05 pin. Nix 2.35 on the runner.
vendorHash / cargoHash so tests do not download.
VM tests need KVM; do not pretend GHA ubuntu has it.
No prod credentials in check.
-L so failures are in the log.

title: Testing in CI Pipelines
text:
Try this

Flip an assertion, nix flake check, restore.
Add curl https://example.com to checkPhase and confirm sandbox failure.
nix flake check twice; second should substitute.
Document whether VM tests run on GHA or on the builder.

title: Secrets Management in CI
text:
Secrets Management in CI
The store is world-readable. CI logs are copied. Fork pull requests are hostile. The boring default is: no secret bytes in Nix; access-tokens for private inputs; Age/sops keys only on trusted jobs; never pull_request_target plus a write token.

title: Secrets Management in CI
text:
Mental model








Kind of secret
Where it lives
How Nix sees it




GitHub PAT for private flakes
Runner nix.conf access-tokens
Fetch, not a derivation input


Age private key for sops
Runner env / SOPS_AGE_KEY
Decrypt at eval/deploy time


DB password for the app
Encrypted in git; decrypted on the host
Path /run/secrets/… only


Cachix write token
Actions secret
cachix push, not flake.nix



Builds should not need production passwords. If nix flake check requires Vault, the check is not hermetic.
trusted push to main
    →  runner gets tokens
    →  nix build   (no app secrets)
    →  deploy      (decrypt on target, not in the NAR)

title: Secrets Management in CI
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Private flake inputs without putting the PAT in Nix
Save as .github/workflows/deploy.yml:
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: cachix/install-nix-action@v27
        with:
          extra_nix_config: |
            access-tokens = github.com=${{ secrets.GH_PAT_FOR_PRIVATE_MODULES }}
      - run: nix flake check
      - run: nix build
access-tokens is daemon config. The token is not hashed into desk-api. Fork PRs must not receive this secret (GitHub’s default for pull_request from forks).


Case 2: Eval sops without decrypting values into the store
# .github/workflows/sops-eval.yml
name: Sops eval
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  eval:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: cachix/install-nix-action@v27
      - name: Eval secret *paths*
        env:
          SOPS_AGE_KEY: ${{ secrets.CI_AGE_PRIVATE_KEY }}
        run: nix eval .#nixosConfigurations.desk-server.config.sops.secrets
The eval prints paths (/run/secrets/db-password), not password strings. If the log shows a password, the module leaked it into config (usually hashedPassword = "plaintext" or environment.FOO = config.sops.secrets.x.path is fine; interpolating builtins.readFile is not).


Case 3: The leak, on purpose, once
Save as leak.nix:
# leak.nix
{ pkgs ? import <nixpkgs> {} }:

pkgs.writeText "database.conf" ''
  password = SuperSecretPassword123
''
nix-build leak.nix
cat result
nix path-info result
Output:
password = SuperSecretPassword123
/nix/store/…-database.conf
Anyone with nix copy of this closure has the password. Delete the file, GC, rotate the password. Then never do this.


Case 4: Cachix write only on main
# .github/workflows/push-cache.yml
name: Push cache
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: cachix/install-nix-action@v27
      - uses: cachix/cachix-action@v15
        with:
          name: desk-cache
          authToken: ${{ secrets.CACHIX_AUTH_TOKEN }}
      - run: nix build
Do not use pull_request_target with this token. A fork can run your workflow against their branch and upload NARs to the team cache.


Case 5: nix flake check without credentials
unset SOPS_AGE_KEY CACHIX_AUTH_TOKEN GH_TOKEN
nix flake check
If this fails because sops cannot decrypt, split checks: eval that only looks at paths and types, versus a deploy job that has keys. Checks that need production secrets will fail on contributor laptops too.

title: Secrets Management in CI
text:
The trap
The trap is builtins.readFile ./prod.key in a module. Eval copies the bytes into the store. nix why-depends /run/current-system will show a path whose cat is the key.
The other trap is printing secrets in set -x bash. echo "$SOPS_AGE_KEY" in a workflow is a rotation event.

title: Secrets Management in CI
text:
The boring rule

Store is public. GitHub logs are public-ish. Treat both as hostile.
access-tokens for fetches. Encrypted files in git for app secrets. Decrypt on the host.
Write tokens (Cachix, deploy keys) only on push to main.
nix flake check without production credentials.
After any leak, rotate. GC does not un-copy a cache.

title: Secrets Management in CI
text:
Try this

Case 3 on a throwaway password. cat $(nix-build leak.nix --no-out-link). Then GC and confirm you still understand copies in the cache if you had pushed.
nix-instantiate --eval -E 'builtins.readFile ./test.txt' with a dummy file. Note that the string is in the eval result.
Confirm nix flake check on a clone with no SOPS_AGE_KEY.
Open the Actions secret list and tick “review logs for accidental echo” on the last deploy job.

title: Remote Builders
text:
Remote Builders
Binary caches move results. Remote builders move work. The boring default is: evaluate on the laptop, realise on a machine that has CPU, KVM, and the right system, then push the result to the team cache.
A laptop should not compile Chromium. A Darwin laptop cannot natively produce x86_64-linux test VMs. Both problems are remote builders, not “more -j”.

title: Remote Builders
text:
Mental model









Binary cache
Remote builder




Needs the path to already exist?
Yes
No


What moves first
NAR (result)
.drv + input paths, then NAR back


Trust
Signing keys
SSH user on the builder


Typical role
Everyone pulls
One beefy box (or a queue) builds



laptop  --drv-->  builder  --push-->  cache  --substitute-->  fleet
nix.buildMachines (NixOS) or --builders (CLI) lists machines:

hostName, sshUser, sshKey
system (x86_64-linux, aarch64-linux, …)
protocol (ssh-ng preferred)
maxJobs, speedFactor
supportedFeatures (kvm, big-parallel, nixos-test)

If a derivation requires kvm and the builder does not advertise it, Nix builds locally (or fails). Mysterious local compiles are often a missing feature flag.

title: Remote Builders
Remote Builders
text:
The trap
The trap is pointing buildMachines at a machine that is also a substituter with a different nixpkgs. You upload inputs, it rebuilds everything because its store is on 23.11. Same flake.lock everywhere; builder substitutes from the team cache (builders-use-substitutes).
The other trap is user SSH config (~/.ssh/config Host aliases) that root’s daemon does not read. Use hostName IPs or put the alias in /root/.ssh/config.

title: Remote Builders
text:
The boring rule

Cache for results, builders for first compiles and foreign system.
ssh-ng, builders-use-substitutes, --max-jobs 0 when you mean “remote only.”
Advertise kvm / nixos-test / big-parallel honestly.
Daemon SSH keys, not your interactive ssh-agent, unless you designed for that.
Builder nixpkgs + cache = laptop flake lock + team cache.

title: Remote Builders
text:
Try this

sudo ssh from Case 3 until nix-store --version prints without a password.
nix build nixpkgs#hello --max-jobs 0 --builders '…' and watch the builder’s nix-daemon log (journalctl -fu nix-daemon).
Remove kvm from supportedFeatures, run a nixosTest, and note where it builds. Put kvm back.
After a remote build, nix path-info -Shr ./result on the laptop — the NAR should have been copied back. Then cachix push so the next laptop never builds it.

title: Creating Container Images with Nix (dockerTools)
text:
Creating Container Images with Nix (dockerTools)
FROM debian:latest plus apt-get is a different closure every Tuesday. The boring default is: pkgs.dockerTools.buildLayeredImage (or streamLayeredImage) from nixpkgs 26.05, no daemon at build time, cacert if you speak TLS.

title: Creating Container Images with Nix (dockerTools)
text:
Mental model
Nix builds an OCI tarball from store paths. Layers split by derivation so glibc stays cached when desk-api changes. No /bin/bash unless you listed pkgs.bash.







Function
Output




buildLayeredImage
.tar.gz you docker load


streamLayeredImage
a script that streams to docker load (smaller eval)



Podman and Docker both load the tarball. Building does not need root.
desk-api drv  +  cacert  →  layered OCI  →  docker load / podman load

title: Creating Container Images with Nix (dockerTools)
Creating Container Images with Nix (dockerTools)
text:
The trap
The trap is forgetting cacert. HTTPS fails with x509: certificate signed by unknown authority. Include pkgs.cacert and SSL_CERT_FILE.
The other trap is contents = [ pkgs.stdenv ]; so “debug is easy.” You just shipped a compiler.

title: Creating Container Images with Nix (dockerTools)
text:
The boring rule

buildLayeredImage / streamLayeredImage. No Dockerfile FROM ubuntu.
Pin tags. Include cacert (and tzdata if you format times).
vendorHash is a FOD. Probe once.
Build in CI without dockerd. Load or skopeo copy after.
Debug images are a different output, not extra packages in prod.

title: Creating Container Images with Nix (dockerTools)
text:
Try this

Build Case 1, tar -tf result | wc -l.
Drop cacert, run a one-liner that curl https://example.com (add curl), read the TLS error, put cacert back.
nix path-info -Shr result and confirm gcc is absent.
Tag 1.0.0 and 1.0.1 after a script change; confirm the base layers’ hashes stayed when only the top layer moved.

title: Kubernetes Manifests as Nix Modules
text:
Kubernetes Manifests as Nix Modules
Hand-written YAML that drifts from the image tag in CI is how Saturday pages start. The boring default is: generate manifests from Nix (same pin as .#image), commit the generated YAML if the cluster cannot eval Nix, and skip Helm until a chart is forced on you.

title: Kubernetes Manifests as Nix Modules
text:
Mental model
Nix can produce JSON/YAML for kubectl apply. Libraries (nixidy, kubenix, or a 40-line writeText) all do the same job: one evaluation, one tag, one registry.
The cluster still runs kubelet. Nix does not replace Kubernetes. It replaces the YAML copypaste.
flake  →  image tag + digest
       →  Deployment YAML with that digest
       →  kubectl apply --server-side
If the platform already speaks Helm only, next chapter. If you own the app, raw manifests are enough.

title: Kubernetes Manifests as Nix Modules
Kubernetes Manifests as Nix Modules
text:
The trap
The trap is templating the image as latest. Every node may run a different digest. Pin tag and digest (image: repo@sha256:…) when the registry supports it.

title: Kubernetes Manifests as Nix Modules
text:
The boring rule

Manifests and image from one flake pin (nixpkgs 26.05).
JSON/YAML generated; apply server-side.
No passwords in ConfigMaps.
Pin digests in production.
Generate-and-commit if GitOps tools cannot eval Nix.

title: Kubernetes Manifests as Nix Modules
text:
Try this

Case 1, jq .spec.replicas result.
Change replicas to 3, rebuild, diff the JSON.
Put image: …:latest in a lab, list why you will not ship it.
Add a Service JSON next to the Deployment in the same file (list of docs or a YAML stream).

title: Helm Charts Generated from Nix
text:
Helm Charts Generated from Nix
Helm is the cluster’s package manager whether you like it or not. The boring default is: pin the chart and the values in Nix (nixhelm / vendored Chart.yaml), render with helm template, and never helm install from floating latest.

title: Helm Charts Generated from Nix
text:
Mental model
A chart is a tarball plus values. Unpinned helm repo add && helm upgrade is npm install on the control plane.



Pin
How




Chart version
chart = { name, repo, version, hash } FOD


Values
Nix attrset → YAML


Image inside values
Same digest as .#image



If the app is yours, prefer raw manifests (previous chapter). Helm when the vendor only ships a chart (ingress-nginx, cert-manager).

title: Helm Charts Generated from Nix
Helm Charts Generated from Nix
text:
The trap
The trap is helm repo update in CI with no version. Monday’s job is not Friday’s chart. Version + hash, like any FOD.

title: Helm Charts Generated from Nix
text:
The boring rule

Helm for vendor charts. Nix manifests for your apps.
Chart tarball in the store (fetchurl + hash) or git-vendor.
Values from Nix. Images from the same flake.
Render in CI; apply the bits you reviewed.
No latest chart, no latest image.

title: Helm Charts Generated from Nix
text:
Try this

helm pull a tiny chart, nix hash path the tgz, put it in fetchurl.
Change replicaCount, re-render, diff.
Break the hash by one character and read the FOD error.
Search CI for helm repo update and delete it.

title: GitOps with Argo CD and Flux
text:
GitOps with Argo CD and Flux
SSH-from-laptop kubectl apply does not scale and does not audit. The boring default is: the cluster pulls generated YAML from git (Flux or Argo), and Nix only runs in CI to refresh that YAML.

title: GitOps with Argo CD and Flux
text:
Mental model



Tool
Pull model




Flux
controllers reconcile GitRepository + Kustomization


Argo CD
Application CR points at a git path



Both want plain YAML in the repo (or a Helm release they render). They do not eval your flake on the control plane. CI:
nix build .#manifests  →  commit generated/  →  Flux applies
Pick one. Running Argo and Flux on the same cluster is a fight.

title: GitOps with Argo CD and Flux
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Generated tree layout
generated/
  desk/
    namespace.yaml
    deploy.yaml
    svc.yaml
nix build .#manifests
rsync -a --delete result/ generated/desk/
git add generated && git diff --cached
Human reviews the YAML, not the Nix, at merge time — or reviews both.


Case 2: Flux GitRepository (illustrative)
Save as generated/flux/gitrepo.yaml:
# gitrepo.yaml
apiVersion: source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: GitRepository
metadata:
  name: desk
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 1m
  url: https://git.desk.internal/platform/desk.git
  ref:
    branch: main
The URL is your repo. Auth is a Secret Flux already knows, not a token in Nix.


Case 3: Kustomization pointing at generated YAML
# kustomization-flux.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Kustomization
metadata:
  name: desk-api
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 5m
  sourceRef:
    kind: GitRepository
    name: desk
  path: ./generated/desk
  prune: true
prune: true deletes objects you removed from git. That is the point. Test in staging first.


Case 4: CI gate
# .github/workflows/manifests.yml
name: manifests
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  gen:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: cachix/install-nix-action@v27
      - run: nix build .#manifests
      - run: diff -ru generated/desk result
If someone edited YAML by hand, the PR fails. Edit Nix, regenerate, commit both.


Case 5: Argo Application (if the org standardised on Argo)
# application.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: desk-api
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://git.desk.internal/platform/desk.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: generated/desk
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: desk
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
Same generated path. Do not point Argo at helm/ with unpinned deps.

title: GitOps with Argo CD and Flux
text:
The trap
The trap is the laptop as GitOps: flux reconcile after kubectl apply after nix build that never got pushed. Git is the desired state. If it is not in main, the cluster should not have it.

title: GitOps with Argo CD and Flux
text:
The boring rule

One GitOps controller. Generated YAML in git. Nix in CI.
diff generated output on every PR.
prune in staging before production.
Secrets still not in that YAML (sops + KSOPS / External Secrets).
Pin git targetRevision to a tag for prod if you need freeze.

title: GitOps with Argo CD and Flux
text:
Try this

diff -ru two nix build .#manifests trees with no edits — empty.
Change a replica count in Nix, regenerate, read the YAML diff as if you were on-call.
Write a one-page “we use Flux xor Argo” note in the desk repo.
Confirm kubectl on your laptop is read against prod, not write (RBAC).

title: Service Mesh and Observability
text:
Service Mesh and Observability
A mesh is another control plane. The boring default is: Prometheus + logs + a NetworkPolicy before Istio; add a mesh only when mTLS between 20+ services is a written requirement.

title: Service Mesh and Observability
text:
Mental model







Need
Boring tool




CPU/RAM/HTTP metrics
prometheus + node_exporter / app /metrics


Logs
journald on NixOS; Loki if you already have it


mTLS inside the cluster
Mesh (Istio/Linkerd) or app TLS


Traffic split
Ingress / Service, then mesh



NixOS can run Prometheus on the ops host without Kubernetes (capstone). In-cluster, same rule: pin charts, generate YAML.
This chapter does not install Istio. It tells you what to measure first so you do not.

title: Service Mesh and Observability
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: App metrics without a mesh
Save as metrics.nix (NixOS ops host):
# metrics.nix
{
  services.prometheus = {
    enable = true;
    scrapeConfigs = [
      {
        job_name = "desk-api";
        static_configs = [ { targets = [ "10.100.0.11:8080" ]; } ];
      }
    ];
  };
}
The Go service exposes /metrics. If it does not, a mesh will not invent useful RED metrics for you.


Case 2: Probe the endpoint
curl -sS http://10.100.0.11:8080/metrics | head
Output (shape):
# HELP go_goroutines Number of goroutines
# TYPE go_goroutines gauge
go_goroutines 7
No output → fix the app, do not add Envoy.


Case 3: NetworkPolicy before sidecar
# netpol.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: desk-api
  namespace: desk
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: desk-api
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: desk-ing
      ports:
        - port: 8080
Generate this from Nix like any manifest. Most “we need a mesh” tickets are “we need NetworkPolicy.”


Case 4: If you must mesh
Pin the Linkerd or Istio chart version + hash (Helm chapter). Inject sidecars in one namespace first. Measure CPU. Roll back with GitOps prune.
Do not enable the mesh globally on day one.


Case 5: Logs on NixOS already exist
journalctl -u desk-api -n 50 --no-pager
Ship them with services.promtail or systemd-journal-upload if you have a Loki. A mesh access log is extra, not a substitute for application logs.

title: Service Mesh and Observability
text:
The trap
The trap is installing Istio to “get observability.” You get a second failure domain, CNI races, and a dashboard. Start with /metrics and NetworkPolicy.

title: Service Mesh and Observability
text:
The boring rule

/metrics on the app. Prometheus scrape config in Nix.
NetworkPolicy before sidecars.
Mesh is optional and pinned. One namespace first.
journalctl is a valid log system.
Do not run two meshes.

title: Service Mesh and Observability
text:
Try this

Hit /metrics on a desk service or add a one-line expvar/prometheus handler in a lab binary.
Write a NetworkPolicy that allows only the ingress pods.
List three problems a mesh does not fix (bad schema, slow SQL, missing auth).
nixos-option services.prometheus.scrapeConfigs on 26.05.

title: Managing Terraform Providers with Nix
text:
Managing Terraform Providers with Nix
terraform init downloading whatever the registry serves this morning is a supply chain. The boring default is: pkgs.opentofu or pkgs.terraform.withPlugins from nixpkgs 26.05 so providers are store paths.
OpenTofu is the next chapter; the wrapper pattern is the same. Prefer OpenTofu on a new desk. This chapter names Terraform because that is the API people google.

title: Managing Terraform Providers with Nix
text:
Mental model
withPlugins builds a Terraform/OpenTofu wrapper whose plugin directory is in /nix/store. init does not need the network for providers. State still lives where you put it (S3, local) — Nix does not replace the backend.
nix develop  →  tofu/terraform in PATH
                 plugins = /nix/store/…-terraform-providers
terraform init -plugin-dir=…  →  offline providers

title: Managing Terraform Providers with Nix
Managing Terraform Providers with Nix
text:
The trap
The trap is terraform init in CI with a clean $HOME and no withPlugins. Registry outage or a yanked version becomes your outage.

title: Managing Terraform Providers with Nix
text:
The boring rule

Providers from nixpkgs (26.05 pin), not the registry at apply time.
which terraform is a store path.
State backend is still your problem (lock table, encryption).
Prefer OpenTofu for new work (next chapter).
Overlay only when you must pin a provider the channel does not have.

title: Managing Terraform Providers with Nix
text:
Try this

Case 1, which terraform, ls $(dirname $(which terraform))/../libexec or equivalent plugin dir.
terraform init with NIX_CURL_TIMEOUT=1 / offline to confirm no download.
Add p.null to the plugin list, enter a new shell, terraform version.
git grep setup-terraform and delete it from CI.

title: OpenTofu Integration
text:
OpenTofu Integration
Terraform’s license change is why OpenTofu exists. The boring default for a new desk is: pkgs.opentofu with withPlugins on nixpkgs 26.05, .tofu or .tf files, same backend discipline.

title: OpenTofu Integration
text:
Mental model
OpenTofu is a Terraform-compatible CLI. Providers from nixpkgs attach the same way. State files from Terraform 1.x often import; test in a clone of state first.
pkgs.opentofu.withPlugins (p: [ p.aws p.random ])
Commands: tofu init|plan|apply. Do not install both Terraform and OpenTofu on PATH without wrapping.

title: OpenTofu Integration
OpenTofu Integration
text:
The trap
The trap is migrating state on Friday in production without tofu plan against a copied state. Clone the backend key, plan, then cut.

title: OpenTofu Integration
text:
The boring rule

New work: OpenTofu from 26.05. withPlugins.
One CLI on PATH.
State credentials are secrets (sops / env), not Nix strings.
fmt + plan in CI. Apply on main with protection.
Test state migration on a copy.

title: OpenTofu Integration
text:
Try this

nix develop --command tofu version and confirm a store path.
tofu plan on random_pet without AWS.
tofu fmt -check on a badly indented file, fix, re-run.
Write down where state lives for the desk (bucket + key) in the repo README — not the credentials.

title: Ansible Provisioning with Nix
text:
Ansible Provisioning with Nix
Ansible mutates hosts. NixOS replaces that for machines you own. The boring default is: do not Ansible a NixOS box; if you must drive a fleet of Ubuntu leftovers, pin pkgs.ansible in a 26.05 devShell and inventory in git.

title: Ansible Provisioning with Nix
text:
Mental model







Host OS
Tool




NixOS
nixos-rebuild / Colmena / nixos-anywhere


Legacy Ubuntu/Debian you cannot reinstall this quarter
Ansible from a Nix shell



Using both on the same NixOS host (ansible ad-hoc apt) fights the next switch.

title: Ansible Provisioning with Nix
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Pinned ansible CLI
# flake.nix
{
  inputs.nixpkgs.url = "github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-26.05";
  outputs = { self, nixpkgs }:
    let
      pkgs = nixpkgs.legacyPackages.x86_64-linux;
    in
    {
      devShells.x86_64-linux.default = pkgs.mkShell {
        packages = [ pkgs.ansible ];
      };
    };
}
nix develop --command ansible --version


Case 2: Inventory in git
Save as inventory.ini:
# inventory.ini
[legacy]
ubuntu-leftover.desk.internal
nix develop --command ansible all -i inventory.ini -m ping


Case 3: Collections pinned, not ansible-galaxy at runtime
# collections.nix
{ pkgs ? import <nixpkgs> {} }:

pkgs.ansible.overrideAttrs (_: {
  # prefer pkgs.ansible with extra collections from nixpkgs when they exist
})
If nixpkgs has the collection as a package, use it. If not, vendor the collection tarball as a FOD into ANSIBLE_COLLECTIONS_PATH. Do not ansible-galaxy install on the runner every job.


Case 4: Playbook that only talks to legacy
Save as ping.yml:
# ping.yml
- hosts: legacy
  gather_facts: false
  tasks:
    - ping:
nix develop --command ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini ping.yml


Case 5: Refuse NixOS in the inventory
# assert.yml
- hosts: all
  tasks:
    - name: skip nixos
      fail:
        msg: "Use nixos-rebuild, not Ansible"
      when: ansible_facts['os_family'] | default('') == 'NixOS'

title: Ansible Provisioning with Nix
text:
The trap
The trap is Ansible copy of a configuration.nix then shell: nixos-rebuild. You now have two sources of truth. SSH to the host and rebuild from the flake, or Colmena.

title: Ansible Provisioning with Nix
text:
The boring rule

NixOS hosts: no Ansible.
Legacy hosts: Ansible from a Nix-pinned CLI + vendored collections.
Inventory in git. No ad-hoc ansible all.
Collections are FODs, not galaxy-on-Monday.
Plan the reinstall to NixOS; Ansible is a bridge.

title: Ansible Provisioning with Nix
text:
Try this

which ansible inside nix develop.
Add a fake inventory host, ansible-inventory --list.
git grep ansible on NixOS modules — should be empty.
Write the retirement date for the last Ubuntu leftover in the desk README.

title: Cloud Provider Configuration
text:
Cloud Provider Configuration
Cloud consoles are mutable. The boring default is: NixOS images from nixos-generators (or official AMIs), cloud-init only for SSH keys at first boot, then the flake owns the instance.

title: Cloud Provider Configuration
text:
Mental model



Piece
Owner




AMI / qcow / gce image
nixos-generators on 26.05, or NixOS AMIs


Instance size, disk, VPC
OpenTofu withPlugins


OS config
nixosConfigurations in the same repo


First-boot SSH
cloud-init / metadata once



Do not bake AWS keys into the image.

title: Cloud Provider Configuration
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Official AMI lookup (OpenTofu)
# ami.tf
data "aws_ami" "nixos" {
  owners      = ["427812963091"]
  most_recent = true
  filter {
    name   = "name"
    values = ["nixos/26.05*"]
  }
  filter {
    name   = "architecture"
    values = ["x86_64"]
  }
}
Owner ID is the NixOS AMI account as documented on nixos.org/download. Confirm it when you copy.


Case 2: Image you built
nix build .#amazon
# upload the VHD / AMI import per AWS docs
The generator chapter produces the artifact. This chapter just consumes the AMI id in tofu.


Case 3: user-data is not configuration.nix
# userdata.tf
user_data = <<-EOT
  # cloud-config
  users:
    - name: deskadmin
      ssh-authorized-keys:
        - ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAI…
EOT
After first boot, Colmena / nixos-rebuild --flake takes over. Do not keep growing user-data with packages.


Case 4: Security group matches the firewall chapter
Open 22 from the office VPN, 443 on the gateway. Do not 0.0.0.0/0 on 22 “for debug.” The NixOS firewall and the cloud SG should tell the same story.


Case 5: Instance tags
tags = {
  Name    = "desk-app-01"
  Flake   = "git.desk.internal/platform/desk"
  HostKey = "app-01"
}
Tags are how you find the box when DNS is wrong. They are not secrets.

title: Cloud Provider Configuration
text:
The trap
The trap is an AMI from 24.11 still in tofu after the flake moved to 26.05. The instance boots old software, then the first rebuild is a surprise kernel. Pin AMI name nixos/26.05* or a specific AMI id you tested.

title: Cloud Provider Configuration
text:
The boring rule

Images: 26.05 generator or official 26.05 AMI.
tofu owns cloud objects. Flake owns the OS.
user-data: SSH keys only.
SG + NixOS firewall agree.
No cloud keys in the image.

title: Cloud Provider Configuration
text:
Try this

aws ec2 describe-images --owners 427812963091 --filters Name=name,Values=nixos/26.05* (if you have AWS) and record an AMI id.
Compare that id to what tofu would pick with most_recent.
Read the generator chapter’s amazon format name on 26.05.
List ports in SG vs networking.firewall.allowedTCPPorts for one host — they should match.

title: Multi-Cloud Deployment Patterns
text:
Multi-Cloud Deployment Patterns
Two clouds is two IAM models, two images, two outages. The boring default is: one cloud until you have a written reason; if you must span, one flake with two nixosConfigurations and two tofu roots — not a unified abstraction layer.

title: Multi-Cloud Deployment Patterns
text:
Mental model
NixOS closures are cloud-agnostic. Images and metadata are not. An AWS AMI is not a GCP image. nixos-generators emits per-format artifacts from the same modules.
modules/desk-api.nix
    ├── nixosConfigurations.desk-aws
    └── nixosConfigurations.desk-gcp
generators: amazon | gce | azure
Do not share state files across clouds.

title: Multi-Cloud Deployment Patterns
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Shared module, two hosts
# hosts.nix
{
  desk-aws = { modules = [ ./common.nix ./aws.nix ]; };
  desk-gcp = { modules = [ ./common.nix ./gcp.nix ]; };
}
common.nix has users, sshd, desk-api. Cloud files have disks and networking the provider needs.


Case 2: stateVersion
# common.nix
{
  system.stateVersion = "26.05";
}
Both clouds, same birth if they were born on 26.05.


Case 3: Images
nixos-amazon-image-26.05.vhd
nixos-gce-image-26.05.tar.gz
Build from the generator chapter. Do not convert an AMI to GCE with a random script if the generator already has gce.


Case 4: Separate tofu directories
tofu/aws/
tofu/gcp/
Different backends. Different credentials. A for_each over {aws, gcp} in one state file is how you lock the wrong cloud.


Case 5: WireGuard between clouds
If the only reason for two clouds is “HA,” a WireGuard mesh (networking chapter) plus Colmena is enough. Multi-cloud Kubernetes is not a first project.

title: Multi-Cloud Deployment Patterns
text:
The trap
The trap is a “cloud-agnostic” Nix wrapper that hides AMI vs GCE differences until apply time. Keep the differences in aws.nix / gcp.nix where you can read them.

title: Multi-Cloud Deployment Patterns
text:
The boring rule

One cloud first.
Same NixOS modules; different image formats and tofu roots.
stateVersion 26.05 on new hosts.
No shared terraform state.
Mesh if you need routing; not a service mesh across clouds on day one.

title: Multi-Cloud Deployment Patterns
text:
Try this

List what actually differs between two clouds for the desk (image, IP, disk).
Draw two tofu dirs on paper. Do not merge them.
Build .#amazon and .#gce from one module set (generator chapter).
Write the one-sentence reason you need the second cloud — or delete the work.

title: Why Secrets Are Hard with Declarative Config
text:
Why Secrets Are Hard with Declarative Config
Nix wants every input in the expression. Attackers want every input too. The boring default is: treat /nix/store as public, never put secret bytes in Nix, and decrypt only onto /run at boot.

title: Why Secrets Are Hard with Declarative Config
text:
Mental model
/nix/store items are world-readable. Binary caches replicate them. CI logs echo eval results. A private git repo does not make a string in configuration.nix private — the next nix copy to a cache, a coworker, or a backup disk copies the secret.



Safe in the flake
Never in the flake




Path /run/secrets/db
Password string


Age public keys
Age private keys


sops file names
Decrypted YAML


hashedPasswordFile = "/persist/…"
initialPassword = "hunter2"



Builds are sandboxed: they cannot prompt you. If a derivation “needs” the production DB password, the design is wrong. Fetch private source with access-tokens. Fetch private runtime secrets on the machine that runs the unit.
git  →  encrypted blob  →  eval knows the path
boot →  decrypt to tmpfs /run/secrets  →  unit EnvironmentFile

title: Why Secrets Are Hard with Declarative Config
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Prove the leak
Save as leak.nix:
# leak.nix
{ pkgs ? import <nixpkgs> {} }:

pkgs.writeText "database.conf" ''
  password = SuperSecretPassword123
''
nix-build leak.nix
cat result
ls -l result
Output:
password = SuperSecretPassword123
-r--r--r-- 1 root root … /nix/store/…-database.conf
Mode r--r--r--. Any local uid can cat it. nix copy --to ssh://untrusted sends it off-box.


Case 2: builtins.readFile is the same leak
Save as read.nix:
# read.nix
builtins.readFile ./prod.password
echo 'hunter2' > prod.password
nix-instantiate --eval read.nix
Output:
"hunter2\n"
The string is now in the eval. If a module interpolates it into a unit, it is in the store. Use this only with public files (a banner, a JSON schema).


Case 3: Reference a runtime path
Save as safe.nix:
# safe.nix
{ config, ... }:

{
  systemd.services.desk-api.serviceConfig = {
    EnvironmentFile = "/run/secrets/desk-api.env";
    DynamicUser = true;
  };
}
Eval contains the path. The file is created at boot by sops-nix / agenix / Vault agent. nix path-info -r /run/current-system should not contain the password.


Case 4: Hashes versus plaintext
hashedPassword = "$6$…" is still in the store. It is an offline crack target, not a live password. Prefer hashedPasswordFile on a 0400 persist path. Never initialPassword.
# hash-ok-ish.nix
{
  users.users.deskadmin.hashedPasswordFile = "/persist/secrets/deskadmin.hash";
}


Case 5: Hunt the closure
# after a switch, on a lab VM — dummy strings only
sudo grep -R "SuperSecret" /nix/store 2>/dev/null | head
nix why-depends /run/current-system /nix/store/…-database.conf
If grep hits, that generation is tainted. Roll back, rotate, GC, and if you pushed a cache, consider the secret public.

title: Why Secrets Are Hard with Declarative Config
text:
The trap
The trap is private GitHub = safe. Clones, Actions artifacts, nix-copy to the team cache, and a laptop left at security all see the store. Encrypt in git (sops/age) so the repo is safe to copy. Decrypt on the host.

title: Why Secrets Are Hard with Declarative Config
text:
The boring rule

Store is public. Write configs as if a stranger can cat every NAR.
Paths in Nix. Bytes on /run (tmpfs) or a 0400 persist file.
No readFile of secrets. No secret strings in environment.
After a leak: rotate, then delete from git history if you must, but assume copies exist.
nix flake check must not need production secret values.

title: Why Secrets Are Hard with Declarative Config
text:
Try this

Case 1, then stat -c '%a %n' $(readlink -f result) — expect 444 or 555 dir.
Put a dummy token in a .nix file, nixos-rebuild dry-build, grep the built unit in the store. Remove it.
git grep -nE 'initialPassword|privateKey =|password =' -- '*.nix' on the desk repo.
Confirm /run/secrets is tmpfs (findmnt /run/secrets or /run) on a sops-enabled host.

title: Using SOPS for Encrypted Configuration (sops-nix)
text:
Using SOPS for Encrypted Configuration (sops-nix)
Secrets that live in a wiki are missing on the next host. The boring default is: SOPS YAML in git (keys visible, values encrypted) and sops-nix decrypting to /run/secrets at boot.

title: Using SOPS for Encrypted Configuration (sops-nix)
text:
Mental model
Mozilla SOPS encrypts values in YAML/JSON. Key names stay plaintext so diffs stay reviewable (database/password: still reads as that path). Recipients are Age keys (or SSH host keys converted with ssh-to-age).
sops-nix is a NixOS module:

Reads defaultSopsFile.
At activation/boot, decrypts with the host Age key (age.keyFile or SSH host key).
Writes files under /run/secrets/… with owner / mode you set.
Units reference config.sops.secrets.<name>.path.

secrets/desk.yaml   (cipher in git)
        │  sops-nix + host age key
        ▼
/run/secrets/database/password   (0400, tmpfs)
        │
        ▼
desk-api EnvironmentFile=

title: Using SOPS for Encrypted Configuration (sops-nix)
Using SOPS for Encrypted Configuration (sops-nix)
text:
The trap
The trap is encrypting only to your laptop Age key. The server cannot decrypt at boot. Always include the host recipient (and the admin laptop, and CI if CI must eval decrypt).
The other trap is age.keyFile on a path that impermanence wipes. Persist /var/lib/sops-nix or use the SSH host key that you already persist.

title: Using SOPS for Encrypted Configuration (sops-nix)
text:
The boring rule

Encrypted YAML in git. Recipients: admins + each host.
Units consume .path, never decrypted strings in Nix.
Host Age key = SSH host key when you can. Persist that key.
Set owner and mode to match the unit.
sops updatekeys when a machine or person is added or revoked.

title: Using SOPS for Encrypted Configuration (sops-nix)
text:
Try this

age-keygen -o /tmp/k.txt, add the public key to .sops.yaml, sops secrets/demo.yaml with hello: world, sops -d secrets/demo.yaml.
ssh-to-age < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub and encrypt a file to that recipient.
Eval .path from a flake that imports sops-nix. Confirm it starts with /run/secrets.
Intentionally omit the host from .sops.yaml, rebuild a VM, read the sops-nix unit log. Add the host and updatekeys.

title: HashiCorp Vault Integration
text:
HashiCorp Vault Integration
sops-nix and age cover static secrets in git. Large desks that already run Vault want short-lived database passwords and certs. The boring default is: Vault Agent on the node, templates to /run/vault, Nix only knows the paths — and if you do not already operate Vault, stay on sops-nix.

title: HashiCorp Vault Integration
text:
Mental model
Vault issues leases. The agent:

Authenticates (AppRole, AWS, Kubernetes — pick one).
Reads secrets / PKI.
Renders a file on tmpfs.
Signals the unit (SIGHUP or restart) when the file changes.

NixOS owns services.vault-agent (or a systemd.services wrapper if the module name differs on your pin — nixos-option services.vault-agent). The role-id can live in the store. The secret-id cannot.
Vault  --lease-->  vault-agent  --template-->  /run/vault/db.env
                                                      │
                                                      ▼
                                              desk-api EnvironmentFile=

title: HashiCorp Vault Integration
HashiCorp Vault Integration
text:
The trap
The trap is a root Vault token in configuration.nix. That token is in the store and in every cache copy. AppRole + a sops-backed secret-id. Never VAULT_TOKEN in the flake.
The other trap is ignoring lease TTL. Agent templates that nobody reloads leave the DB password valid in Vault’s eyes for twenty minutes after the process started — then Postgres rejects it at 3 a.m.

title: HashiCorp Vault Integration
text:
The boring rule

Nix knows addresses, role ids, and paths. Bytes stay in Vault and /run.
AppRole (or cloud auth). No root tokens in git.
Reload or restart on template change.
secret-id via sops-nix. role-id may be public.
Skip Vault if sops-nix already solves the desk.

title: HashiCorp Vault Integration
text:
Try this

nixos-option services.vault-agent (or rg vault-agent in nixpkgs) on a 26.05 pin and write down the module path your release actually ships.
Render a dummy db.ctmpl with static {{ printf "x" }} locally using consul-template / vault agent -dev if you have a lab Vault. Confirm the output file is not a store path.
git grep VAULT_TOKEN on the desk repo. It should be empty.
Time a database lease TTL and confirm desk-api restarts before expiry in the lab.

title: Age Encryption for Simple Secrets
text:
Age Encryption for Simple Secrets
GPG keyrings and expiry theatre do not belong in a desk CI job. The boring default is: age (X25519) for files, ssh-to-age so SSH keys are recipients, and agenix only if you want NixOS decryption without SOPS’s YAML.
This book already uses sops-nix as the default for structured secrets. Age is the primitive underneath. Agenix is the alternative when you want one file per secret and less YAML.

title: Age Encryption for Simple Secrets
text:
Mental model







Tool
Role




age
Encrypt/decrypt bytes to age1… or SSH recipients


ssh-to-age
Convert ssh-ed25519 pubkey → age1…


agenix
NixOS module: .age files in git → /run/agenix/… at boot



No keyserver. A public key is a line of text. Lose the private key, lose the files (unless another recipient remains).
desk-token.age   (cipher, git)
   recipients: alice's ssh, desk-node host ssh
        │  agenix at boot
        ▼
/run/agenix/desk-token

title: Age Encryption for Simple Secrets
Age Encryption for Simple Secrets
text:
The trap
The trap is one recipient: your laptop. The server is not you. Always include the host SSH key.
The other trap is using both sops-nix and agenix for the same secret. Pick one tree: sops YAML for many keys, agenix for a handful of files. Two systems means two rekey rituals.

title: Age Encryption for Simple Secrets
text:
The boring rule

Age, not GPG, for desk secrets.
Recipients = people + hosts (ssh-to-age).
Rekey when keys are added or revoked.
Private keys never in git. Ciphertext always in git.
Prefer sops-nix if you already have YAML; agenix if you want one-file-one-secret.

title: Age Encryption for Simple Secrets
text:
Try this

ssh-to-age < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub, encrypt a one-line file, decrypt with -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.
Encrypt to two recipients, remove your key from the list, confirm decrypt fails, put it back.
agenix -e a dummy secret in a throwaway repo and git add only the .age file.
On a VM, omit the host from publicKeys, switch, read journalctl -u agenix. Add the host, rekey, switch again.

title: Security Hardening Patterns
text:
Security Hardening Patterns
Open ports, writable /, and JIT-friendly sysctls are the defaults of a general-purpose distro. The boring default on a desk server is: firewall on, DynamicUser + ProtectSystem=strict on custom units, a small sysctl set, and no hardening that you have not booted.

title: Security Hardening Patterns
text:
Mental model
Defense in this book is already mostly done if you followed earlier chapters: immutable store, listed firewall ports, no plaintext secrets, SSH keys only. This chapter is the extra kernel/unit knobs.







Layer
Boring control




Network
networking.firewall.enable = true;


Units
ProtectSystem, ProtectHome, NoNewPrivileges, DynamicUser


Kernel
boot.kernel.sysctl for kptr, bpf, syncookies


Firmware
microcode (hardware chapter)


Audit
systemd-analyze security <unit>



MemoryDenyWriteExecute = true breaks Node, JVM, and some Python. Test, then enable. A unit that will not start is not hardened; it is down.

title: Security Hardening Patterns
Security Hardening Patterns
text:
The trap
The trap is copying a 40-line hardening gist onto every unit, including ones that need /home, BPF, or devices. The activation succeeds; the service dies; you disable the firewall to “debug.” Add flags one at a time. Keep the firewall on.

title: Security Hardening Patterns
text:
The boring rule

Firewall, keys, secrets, and an immutable store first. Sysctls second.
DynamicUser + ProtectSystem=strict on your network daemons.
MemoryDenyWriteExecute only after the app starts under it.
ip_forward only on routers.
systemd-analyze security as a diff tool, not a scoreboard.

title: Security Hardening Patterns
text:
Try this

systemd-analyze security desk-api before and after Case 1. Note which checks flipped.
Set MemoryDenyWriteExecute = true on a Node unit in a VM, start it, read the journal, set it false.
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward on a worker vs the gateway.
systemctl cat nginx on 26.05 and list sandbox flags the module already set.

title: The Internal Developer Platform Pattern
text:
The Internal Developer Platform Pattern
Fifty repos each pinning their own nixpkgs is fifty llvm builds. The boring default is: one platform flake on nixpkgs 26.05 that exports devShells, templates, and nixosModules, and product flakes follows it.

title: The Internal Developer Platform Pattern
text:
Mental model
github:desk/platform   nixpkgs 26.05
    ├── devShells.backend / frontend
    ├── templates.go-service
    └── nixosModules.baseline
github:desk/desk-api
    inputs.platform.url = …
    inputs.nixpkgs.follows = "platform/nixpkgs"
Upgrading Go or sshd defaults is a platform bump, then a lock bump in each consumer (or a bot). Not a meeting.

title: The Internal Developer Platform Pattern
The Internal Developer Platform Pattern
text:
The trap
The trap is a platform that overlays half of nixpkgs. Consumers cannot debug. Keep the platform thin: shells, templates, 20 lines of sshd. Overlays for one pin, documented.

title: The Internal Developer Platform Pattern
text:
The boring rule

One nixpkgs: 26.05 via the platform flake.
Templates + follows.
nix flake update platform is the upgrade API.
Tags, not floating main, for production consumers.
Thin modules. No mega-overlay.

title: The Internal Developer Platform Pattern
text:
Try this

nix flake init -t from a local path template.
nix flake metadata on a consumer and confirm a single nixpkgs.
Add a devShells.docs with pkgs.mdbook (or pkgs.pandoc) on the platform; consume it.
Tag a fake platform-26.05.3 and pin it in a consumer lock.

title: Monorepo Strategies with Nix
text:
Monorepo Strategies with Nix
A monorepo with src = ./.; on every package rebuilds the world per commit. The boring default is: one flake, many packages.*, lib.fileset / cleanSourceWith per leaf, and CI that builds .#checks not .#everything on a docs-only PR.

title: Monorepo Strategies with Nix
text:
Mental model







Layout
Nix




apps/desk-api
packages.desk-api with src filtered to that tree


apps/desk-web
sibling package; docs change does not rebuild api


modules/
nixosModules


flake.nix
one lock, nixpkgs 26.05



nix flake check should be cheap enough to run on every PR. Heavy images are extra jobs.

title: Monorepo Strategies with Nix
Monorepo Strategies with Nix
text:
The trap
The trap is src = ./.; at repo root for every callPackage. A README typo rebuilds Go. Filter.

title: Monorepo Strategies with Nix
text:
The boring rule

One flake, one 26.05 lock.
Per-package src filters.
Leaf builds on leaf PRs; flake.lock PRs run full check.
No recursive flakes.
vendorHash / cargo hashes per package.

title: Monorepo Strategies with Nix
text:
Try this

nix build .#desk-api then touch a web-only file; --dry-run the api (should be empty if filtered).
lib.fileset vs cleanSource — pick one style per repo.
Add a checks attr that is linkFarm of two packages.
Time nix flake show on the monorepo; if it is minutes, you eval too much at the top.

title: Multi-Platform Development and Distribution
text:
Multi-Platform Development and Distribution
x86_64-linux CI does not prove aarch64-darwin. The boring default is: eachDefaultSystem (or genAttrs) for packages/devShells, native builders for foreign system, and no QEMU-on-the-laptop as the production path.

title: Multi-Platform Development and Distribution
text:
Mental model







What
How




Same shell on Mac + Linux
devShells.${system} from 26.05


Linux binary from a Mac
Remote Linux builder (ssh-ng)


Raspberry Pi
aarch64-linux builder or nixos-generators sd-aarch64



pkgsCross is cross. Remote builder is native. Native is faster and hits the team cache.

title: Multi-Platform Development and Distribution
Multi-Platform Development and Distribution
text:
The trap
The trap is system = "x86_64-linux" hardcoded in a flake used on Apple silicon. Eval may work; go is the wrong ELF. Use eachDefaultSystem or builtins.currentSystem only inside impure nix-shell, not in flakes.

title: Multi-Platform Development and Distribution
text:
The boring rule

Enumerate systems. 26.05 pin.
Native remote builders for foreign Linux.
CI matrix for the OS humans actually use.
Do not plan on x86_64-darwin past 26.05.
Two archs = two cache objects.

title: Multi-Platform Development and Distribution
text:
Try this

nix flake show and list systems.
On a Mac, file $(nix develop --command which go) — should be arm64 if you are on Apple silicon.
nix build --system aarch64-linux without a builder and read the error.
Note 26.11 darwin x86_64 drop in the version appendix.

title: Build Optimization and Performance Tuning
text:
Build Optimization and Performance Tuning
Waiting on eval is not a personality. The boring default is: substituters, auto-optimise-store, filtered src, enough max-jobs, and nix --eval-profiler only when a flake takes minutes to start.

title: Build Optimization and Performance Tuning
text:
Mental model



Slow part
Fix




Download
Team cache, builders-use-substitutes


Compile
Remote builder, max-jobs, don’t rebuild gcc


Eval
Fewer IFDs, fileset, don’t import the monorepo ten times


Disk
GC window, optimise



nix.nrBuildUsers / max-jobs default is fine on a laptop. CI runners with 8 cores should set max-jobs = 8.

title: Build Optimization and Performance Tuning
Build Optimization and Performance Tuning
text:
The trap
The trap is max-jobs = 1 copied from a gist “to reduce RAM” on a 64G builder, then blaming Nix for being slow.

title: Build Optimization and Performance Tuning
text:
The boring rule

Cache first. Jobs/cores second. Eval hygiene third.
No IFD in the hot path.
--dry-run is a perf tool.
Heavy compiles on the builder.
26.05 auto-optimise-store on.

title: Build Optimization and Performance Tuning
text:
Try this

nix show-config | grep max-jobs.
--dry-run before/after a README edit.
Time nix flake show vs nix build on a cached package.
Enable auto-optimise-store if it is off.

title: Debugging and Troubleshooting Production Issues
text:
Debugging and Troubleshooting Production Issues
“It works on my laptop” is a missing nix path-info. The boring default is: nix log, journalctl, nix why-depends, --show-trace, and rollback — in that order — before editing the live unit.

title: Debugging and Troubleshooting Production Issues
text:
Mental model



Symptom
First tool




Build failed
nix log /nix/store/…drv


Eval failed
--show-trace, nix repl .#


Unit failed after switch
journalctl -u, systemctl status


Closure too fat
nix path-info -Shr, why-depends


Host will not boot
previous generation in systemd-boot



You do not vim /etc/systemd/system/foo.service. The next switch undoes it.

title: Debugging and Troubleshooting Production Issues
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Build log
nix build .#desk-api --print-build-logs
nix log .#desk-api
The log is in the store. CI can nix log the same drv.


Case 2: Eval trace
nix eval .#nixosConfigurations.app-01.config.networking.hostName --show-trace
Read the last frame first. Infinite recursion is usually rec + self-reference (language chapter).


Case 3: Unit
systemctl status desk-api --no-pager
journalctl -u desk-api -n 80 --no-pager
systemctl cat desk-api
cat shows the store path. If someone systemctl edit’d, you will see a drop-in — delete it and put the flag in Nix.


Case 4: Why is python in the closure?
nix why-depends /run/current-system $(nix path-info nixpkgs#python3)
Cut the edge (wrapper, propagated input, a script shebang).


Case 5: Rollback
sudo nixos-rebuild switch --rollback
# or at the bootloader: previous NixOS 26.05 generation
Then git revert the flake commit so the next switch does not re-apply the foot-gun.

title: Debugging and Troubleshooting Production Issues
text:
The trap
The trap is fixing production with systemctl edit and a reboot “to see.” You now have unmanaged state. Impermanence will eat it; a persistent root will lie to the next Colmena apply.

title: Debugging and Troubleshooting Production Issues
text:
The boring rule

Logs in the store and journald. Not screenshots of a terminal.
--show-trace for eval. why-depends for size.
Rollback first, bisect the flake second.
No live unit drop-ins.
26.05 nix log / nix path-info are enough; no extra APM required to start.

title: Debugging and Troubleshooting Production Issues
text:
Try this

nix build a deliberately broken runCommand (false) and nix log it.
systemctl cat sshd and find /nix/store.
--rollback on a lab VM after a hostname change.
why-depends hello vs gcc — gcc should not appear in the runtime closure.

title: Testing Strategies for Nix Configurations
text:
Testing Strategies for Nix Configurations
nixos-rebuild switch on prod is not a test. The boring default is: nix flake check on every PR, pkgs.testers.runNixOSTest (or nixosTest) for services that listen, and a VM that is not the laptop.

title: Testing Strategies for Nix Configurations
text:
Mental model



Level
Command




Eval
nix eval, types


Build
nix build .#desk-api


NixOS VM
nixosTest / runNixOSTest


Full check
nix flake check



VM tests need kvm on the builder (remote-builders supportedFeatures). Darwin laptops offload them.

title: Testing Strategies for Nix Configurations
Testing Strategies for Nix Configurations
text:
The trap
The trap is a 20-node test on every PR. Keep PR tests under a few minutes. Nightly runs the farm.

title: Testing Strategies for Nix Configurations
text:
The boring rule

flake check on PR. VM tests when a unit listens.
KVM on the builder. 26.05 runNixOSTest.
No network in checkPhase.
Small PR tests; big nightly.
A test that needs prod credentials is not a check.

title: Testing Strategies for Nix Configurations
text:
Try this

nix flake check on the desk flake.
Run Case 2 (needs KVM).
Add a failing assert in testScript and confirm non-zero exit.
nixos-option nothing — write one checks attr that builds .#desk-api.

title: Maintenance, Upgrades, and Migration
text:
Maintenance, Upgrades, and Migration
nix flake update on Friday without a plan is a weekend. The boring default is: pin nixos-26.05, bump in a dedicated PR, nix flake check + one lab host, then Colmena — and never bump stateVersion as part of that PR.

title: Maintenance, Upgrades, and Migration
text:
Mental model



Move
What changes




nix flake update nixpkgs
Same release train, newer commits


nixos-25.11 → nixos-26.05
Release upgrade. Read the notes.


stateVersion
Almost never



25.11 is EOL (2026-06-30). New hosts: 26.05. Old hosts: change the input, keep stateVersion.

title: Maintenance, Upgrades, and Migration
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Lock bump inside 26.05
nix flake update nixpkgs
nix flake metadata
nix flake check
sudo nixos-rebuild dry-activate --flake .#desk-lab
Read unit restarts. Then switch the lab. Then the fleet.


Case 2: Release upgrade
# flake.nix
inputs.nixpkgs.url = "github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-26.05";
was nixos-25.11. git diff flake.lock is huge. That is expected. Run VM tests. Read nixos.org 26.05 notes (systemd stage-1 default, module renames).


Case 3: stateVersion stays
system.stateVersion = "25.11"; # host born on 25.11
Still correct on a 26.05 channel. Do not “tidy” it to "26.05" in the same PR.


Case 4: Home Manager follows
inputs.home-manager.url = "github:nix-community/home-manager/release-26.05";
inputs.home-manager.inputs.nixpkgs.follows = "nixpkgs";
Mismatch (HM 24.11 + nixpkgs 26.05) is eval pain. Same release train.


Case 5: Record
# CHANGELOG.md
- 2026-09-09: nixpkgs 26.05.9440 on lab, then app-01
If you cannot say which lock is in prod, you cannot roll back with confidence.

title: Maintenance, Upgrades, and Migration
text:
The trap
The trap is changing stateVersion to match the channel. Postgres dirs, user state, and module defaults then migrate. Channel bump ≠ stateVersion bump.

title: Maintenance, Upgrades, and Migration
text:
The boring rule

26.05 is the current train. Update locks in PRs.
Lab host first. Fleet second.
stateVersion is birth.
HM release matches nixpkgs release.
Changelog the lock.

title: Maintenance, Upgrades, and Migration
text:
Try this

nix flake metadata and write the locked nixpkgs date.
dry-activate on a lab after a lock bump.
Find stateVersion in the repo; confirm none were “updated” to 26.05 on old hosts without notes.
Read the 26.05 release notes once; list one module that might affect the desk.

title: Enterprise Operational Checklists
text:
Enterprise Operational Checklists
A wiki page of “remember to” is how generations rot. The boring default is: short checklists in the repo, run as commands (flake check, restic snapshots, colmena apply --dry-run), not as a PDF.

title: Enterprise Operational Checklists
text:
Mental model
If it is not a command, it will not happen. Each item below maps to a chapter you already have.

title: Enterprise Operational Checklists
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Daily (human)
# desk-daily.sh
nix flake check
systemctl --failed --no-pager
df -h /nix /boot /persist


Case 2: Weekly
sudo nix-collect-garbage --delete-older-than 14d
sudo nix-store --optimise
sudo restic snapshots   # or systemctl status restic-backups-desk


Case 3: Before a fleet apply
git log -1 --oneline
nix flake metadata
nix flake check
colmena apply --dry-run
Then apply one host, then the rest.


Case 4: After a security advisory
nix flake update nixpkgs
nix flake check
# lab switch, then fleet
Do not wait for the quarterly bump if the advisory is in nixpkgs.


Case 5: New host

Disko by-id + LUKS + @persist
sops recipient + rekey
stateVersion = "26.05"
WireGuard IP allocated in git
restic include list
nixos-anywhere once
Colmena tag

title: Enterprise Operational Checklists
text:
The trap
The trap is a 90-line checklist nobody runs. Five commands in scripts/ beat a Confluence page.

title: Enterprise Operational Checklists
text:
The boring rule

Commands in git. 26.05. sops. restic. Colmena.
Dry-run before apply.
14-day GC. ESP configurationLimit.
New hosts born on 26.05.
Advisories: lock bump, not hope.

title: Enterprise Operational Checklists
text:
Try this

Put Case 1 in scripts/desk-daily.sh and run it.
Time nix flake check. If it is >10 minutes, split checks.
Confirm restic last snapshot is < 48h on the lab.
Walk Case 5 against a throwaway VM.

title: Fleet Deployments with Colmena
text:
Fleet Deployments with Colmena
for h in hosts; do nixos-rebuild --flake .#$h; done forgets --target-host flags. The boring default is: Colmena (or deploy-rs) with one hive file, SSH from ops-01, and --on for canaries.

title: Fleet Deployments with Colmena
text:
Mental model
Colmena reads nixosConfigurations (or a hive.nix) and SSHes the closure. Build locally or on a builder, copy, activate. Same 26.05 lock as the laptop.
ops-01  colmena apply --on app-01
             │
             ▼
        app-01 nixos-rebuild switch  (remote)

title: Fleet Deployments with Colmena
Fleet Deployments with Colmena
text:
The trap
The trap is applying all hosts in parallel on a shared DB migration. Serial the stateful node. Parallel the stateless apps.

title: Fleet Deployments with Colmena
text:
The boring rule

One hive. 26.05. SSH from ops.
Canary --on.
Dry-run first.
Stateful hosts serial.
Rollback is the previous generation, then a git revert.

title: Fleet Deployments with Colmena
text:
Try this

colmena --help in a nix shell nixpkgs#colmena.
Apply to a single lab VM.
Break a unit, apply, --rollback on the VM, then revert git.
List which hosts may be parallel in docs/fleet.md.

title: Lightweight MicroVMs with microvm.nix
text:
Lightweight MicroVMs with microvm.nix
Full libvirt guests are slow to iterate. The boring default for local multi-node tests is: microvm.nix (or nixosTest) on 26.05; production still gets real machines or the capstone VMs.

title: Lightweight MicroVMs with microvm.nix
text:
Mental model
microvm.nix defines a NixOS guest that boots in hundreds of milliseconds, often sharing the host store via virtiofs. It is not a security boundary as strong as a separate hypervisor with its own disks — do not put untrusted tenants there without reading the project docs.
host flake
  nixosConfigurations.desk-micro
    microvm.hypervisor = "qemu"; # or cloud-hypervisor

title: Lightweight MicroVMs with microvm.nix
Lightweight MicroVMs with microvm.nix
text:
The trap
The trap is running production desk-api in a microVM on someone’s laptop. Prod is Colmena to real hosts. microVMs are a lab accelerator.

title: Lightweight MicroVMs with microvm.nix
text:
The boring rule

26.05 + follows.
QEMU/KVM for labs. nixosTest for CI.
No production tenants on a laptop hypervisor.
stateVersion 26.05 on new guests.
Share the store only when you understand the trust model.

title: Lightweight MicroVMs with microvm.nix
text:
Try this

Enable KVM, run a hello microVM.
systemctl status sshd inside it.
Compare boot time to a libvirt NixOS guest.
Add a nixosTest that covers the same sshd enablement instead.

title: Content-Addressed Nix Internals
text:
Content-Addressed Nix Internals
Everyday Nix is input-addressed: the .drv hash names the output. Content-addressed (CA) derivations hash the bytes. The boring default is: keep input-addressed builds; use FODs (fetchurl) for the CA you already need; do not flip contentAddressed on the desk laptop.

title: Content-Addressed Nix Internals
text:
Mental model
You met this in the store-model chapter. Recap:








Kind
Name comes from
Daily use




Input-addressed
.drv
Packages, NixOS


FOD
Declared output hash
Fetchers, vendorHash


Experimental CA
Output hash of normal builds
Labs, nixpkgs experiments



FODs already share identical tarballs. Experimental CA tries to share identical build outputs when two .drvs differ only in comments. It is not the 26.05 workstation default.

title: Content-Addressed Nix Internals
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: FOD is enough
pkgs.fetchurl {
  url = "https://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/hello/hello-2.12.1.tar.gz";
  hash = "sha256-…";
}
Same hash, same path, any URL mirror.


Case 2: Input-addressed comment rebuild
A runCommand with a changed comment is a new path even if cat $out matches. That is normal. Live with it.


Case 3: nix show-derivation
nix show-derivation $(nix-instantiate -E '(import <nixpkgs> {}).hello')
Look at outputs.out.hash vs its absence. FODs have outputHash. hello does not.


Case 4: When CA helps a farm
Hydra with CA can dedup two gcc invocations that produced the same bits. You are not Hydra. Do not enable sandbox-content-addressed because a blog post did.


Case 5: 2.35 lazy flake copy is not CA
Nix 2.35 copies flake sources lazily. That is eval performance, not content-addressed builds. Do not confuse the two in an incident doc.

title: Content-Addressed Nix Internals
text:
The trap
The trap is __contentAddressed = true on a production module “to save disk.” Cache hits become mysterious; nixpkgs support assumes input-addressed. Use --optimise and GC instead.

title: Content-Addressed Nix Internals
text:
The boring rule

FODs for fetches. Input-addressed for builds.
nix-store --optimise for disk.
No experimental CA on desk hosts.
2.35 lazy copy ≠ CA.
Read show-derivation when a path type is unclear.

title: Content-Addressed Nix Internals
text:
Try this

nix show-derivation on hello and on a fetchurl. Compare outputHash.
Change a comment in runCommand, instantiate, confirm new .drv.
nix-store --optimise --dry-run if available, or run optimise on a lab.
git grep contentAddressed — should be empty in the desk flake.

title: Production Architecture and Threat Model
text:
Production Architecture and Threat Model
Toy VMs taught the pieces. The capstone is one desk fleet on NixOS 26.05: four roles, WireGuard, ephemeral workers, sops-nix, Colmena. The boring default is: write the threat model first, then the flake — not a mesh of tools looking for a problem.

title: Production Architecture and Threat Model
text:
Mental model



Production Capstone Fleet Architecture





Host
Role




gw-01
Caddy, ACME, nftables; WireGuard 10.100.0.1


app-01, app-02
desk-api; tmpfs root; DynamicUser


db-01
PostgreSQL; Disko LUKS + Btrfs; /persist


ops-01
Colmena, Prometheus, sops key broker



Invariants:

No secret bytes in git or /nix/store.
Store is read-only. Payloads in /etc die on reboot (workers).
WireGuard for all east-west. No DB port on the public NIC.
flake.lock on nixos-26.05; rollback is a generation, not a restore CD.
Backups of /persist (restic), not of /nix/store.

title: Production Architecture and Threat Model
Production Architecture and Threat Model
text:
The trap
The trap is starting with Istio and three clouds before SSH keys persist across reboot. Finish Disko, impermanence, sops, WireGuard, Colmena, restic. In that order (chapters 2–5).

title: Production Architecture and Threat Model
text:
The boring rule

26.05 lock. Five hosts. One mesh. One secret system (sops).
Public surface is 443 (+ 22 if you must, from a tight SG).
/persist is the backup. Store is the cache.
Rollback is a generation.
Write the threat model in git.

title: Production Architecture and Threat Model
text:
Try this

Copy the host table into your flake as comments. Fill module file names.
List every port you think is open; compare to firewall + cloud SG later.
Name the restic repository in docs/threats.md.
Confirm stateVersion will be "26.05" on new metal.

title: Disko Storage and Ephemeral Base System
text:
Disko Storage and Ephemeral Base System
Every node in our production fleet must deploy onto clean physical or cloud storage without manual partitioning tools. In this chapter, we create the unified Disko storage specification and configure the ephemeral root filesystem with Impermanence.

title: Disko Storage and Ephemeral Base System
text:
Mental model

Unified disk module (disk-layout.nix): Disko formats the physical NVMe or virtual disk into an EFI system partition (/boot) and a LUKS2 encrypted partition.
Btrfs subvolumes on LUKS: Inside the decrypted container, Btrfs subvolumes are created for @nix (the store), @persist (stateful data), and @swap.
RAM root (tmpfs): The root filesystem (/) is mounted in RAM with mode=755,size=2G. Unmounted state is discarded on power-down.
Impermanence persistence: System state required across reboots (SSH host keys, machine-id, WireGuard identity) is bound into /persist.

title: Disko Storage and Ephemeral Base System
Disko Storage and Ephemeral Base System
text:
The trap
The trap is failing to mark /persist as neededForBoot = true. During early boot, the initramfs must mount /persist before systemd starts generating symlinks for machine-id and SSH keys. Always ensure /persist is mounted before root pivot.

title: Disko Storage and Ephemeral Base System
text:
The boring rule

Model all partition tables and filesystems in Disko.
Keep / on tmpfs to enforce declarative purity and eliminate state rot.
Explicitly list all persistent files and directories under /persist.

title: Disko Storage and Ephemeral Base System
text:
Try this

Run nix run github:nix-community/disko -- --mode mount ./modules/disk-layout.nix in a test environment.
Confirm with mount | grep tmpfs that root is mounted on RAM.

title: Hardened Networking and WireGuard Mesh
text:
Hardened Networking and WireGuard Mesh
Exposing internal services, databases, or management endpoints to public IP addresses is an extreme security risk. The boring default is: linking all cluster nodes into a point-to-point encrypted WireGuard mesh on private subnet 10.100.0.0/24, backed by strict nftables firewall policies that drop all unsolicited public traffic.

title: Hardened Networking and WireGuard Mesh
text:
Mental model

Overlay mesh: Each node possesses a static WireGuard private key and an assigned IP (gw-01: 10.100.0.1, app-01: 10.100.0.11, app-02: 10.100.0.12, db-01: 10.100.0.21, ops-01: 10.100.0.30).
Declarative peers: Peer public keys and allowed IPs are configured directly in Nix expressions. WireGuard interfaces establish bidirectional encrypted tunnels instantly on boot.
nftables isolation: The firewall allows public access only on the gateway for ports 80/443. All other node traffic must originate from within the wg0 interface.

title: Hardened Networking and WireGuard Mesh
Hardened Networking and WireGuard Mesh
text:
The trap
The trap is generating WireGuard private keys into /nix/store. Private keys must be created on the host or provisioned via sops-nix directly to /run/secrets/wireguard/private.key.

title: Hardened Networking and WireGuard Mesh
text:
The boring rule

Bind internal services exclusively to the WireGuard mesh interface (wg0).
Restrict public ports to HTTP/HTTPS on the edge gateway and UDP 51820 on peers.
Use persistent keepalives (persistentKeepalive = 25) to maintain NAT traversal across cloud firewalls.

title: Hardened Networking and WireGuard Mesh
text:
Try this

Bring up two test nodes on WireGuard and verify connectivity with ping 10.100.0.21.
Verify with nmap that PostgreSQL port 5432 is closed on the public interface.

title: Distributed Application Stack and Secrets
text:
Distributed Application Stack and Secrets
With storage and networking established, we deploy the production workload: an edge Caddy reverse proxy with automated Let’s Encrypt TLS certificates, a containerless Go microservice with systemd sandboxing, a hardened PostgreSQL 16 database, and SOPS-nix runtime secret distribution.

title: Distributed Application Stack and Secrets
text:
Mental model

Caddy Ingress (gw-01): Terminates TLS, enforces modern ciphers (TLS 1.3), and round-robin proxies requests across backend worker nodes over the WireGuard mesh (10.100.0.11:8080, 10.100.0.12:8080).
Hardened Microservice (app-01, app-02): Runs the compiled application binary as a dynamic unprivileged user with complete systemd sandboxing.
SOPS-nix runtime decryption: Encrypted secrets in git (secrets/cluster.yaml) are decrypted into /run/secrets/ at boot time using the node’s private Age key.

title: Distributed Application Stack and Secrets
Distributed Application Stack and Secrets
text:
The trap
The trap is allowing the web service to talk to the database with unencrypted credentials in command line arguments (--password=secret). Any unprivileged user running ps aux can read arguments of other processes. Always pass credentials via EnvironmentFile mounted from /run/secrets/.

title: Distributed Application Stack and Secrets
text:
The boring rule

Terminate TLS with Caddy for zero-maintenance ACME certificate renewals.
Sandbox every microservice with DynamicUser = true and ProtectSystem = "strict".
Inject secrets exclusively via /run/secrets/ with SOPS-nix.

title: Distributed Application Stack and Secrets
text:
Try this

Run systemd-analyze security desk-api and observe the near-zero exposure rating.
Verify that querying http://localhost:8080/healthz returns HTTP 200 OK.

title: Automated Fleet Rollout and Disaster Recovery
text:
Automated Fleet Rollout and Disaster Recovery
A production architecture is only as dependable as its operational playbook. In this final chapter, we bring the entire cluster to life: orchestrating fleet-wide deployments with Colmena, executing automated canary health checks, and performing a zero-touch bare-metal disaster recovery from scratch.

title: Automated Fleet Rollout and Disaster Recovery
text:
Mental model

The Flake as the cluster source of truth: The root flake.nix declares all nodes, their disk layouts, network identities, and services.
Automated fleet rollouts: Colmena pushes new system closures across the entire fleet in parallel.
Canary deployment pipeline: Colmena updates app-01 first. If health probes on https://api.company.internal/healthz fail, the deployment immediately halts and rolls back before app-02 or the database are touched.
Zero-touch disaster recovery: If a physical server burns down, booting a replacement into rescue mode and running one nixos-anywhere command completely reconstructs the machine in under 4 minutes.

title: Automated Fleet Rollout and Disaster Recovery
Automated Fleet Rollout and Disaster Recovery
text:
The trap
The trap is not testing disaster recovery until a production incident occurs. Schedule automated recovery drills quarterly: wipe a staging server completely and run nixos-anywhere to prove your declarative configurations remain 100% self-sufficient.

title: Automated Fleet Rollout and Disaster Recovery
text:
The boring rule

Model the entire multi-node cluster inside a single Colmena flake.
Enforce canary node verification before rolling out cluster-wide updates.
Verify that every server can be rebuilt from scratch with a single nixos-anywhere command.

title: Automated Fleet Rollout and Disaster Recovery
text:
Try this

Run colmena eval locally to verify that all four cluster nodes evaluate without errors.
